summary: Discovery-style POC scoping to decide Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for latency-sensitive customer facing features. Focus on success criteria, workload sizing, benchmarks, and a 4-6 week pilot timeline. Main concerns: tail latency, cost per token at scale, VPC/KMS integration, and audit logs for compliance.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call - I'm Jordan, AE - Priya is our SE.
[00:06] Carlos (Emberline): Hi yep Carlos here, head of ML. Asha, Tom, Mei and Ben are on too.
[00:12] Priya (Redwood SE): Hey all, glad to be here. Goal for today is to map success criteria and nail down benchmarking so we can recommend Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for your use case.
[00:23] Carlos: Right. High level - we want live-ish user features in customer support routing, sub-second or at least p95 under 400ms if possible. But cost matters, we have seasonal spikes up to 3x.
[00:35] Asha (Infra): Network is a constraint. We need VPC peering and strict egress limits; anything that leaks data out is a no. Also SOC2 and internal audit want KMS/HSM for key management.
[00:48] Priya: Good callouts. So three hosting options: Hosted (fastest to launch, Redwood-managed), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools with isolation), Private (VPC/on-prem with customer control). Each has tradeoffs on latency, cost, and integrations.
[01:05] Tom (Procurement): TCO is big for us. If Dedicated reduces unit cost by 30% at our commit level it's attractive; but procurement lead time for Dedicated is longer.
[01:15] Mei (Security): We need audit logs, SSO/SAML, and encryption-in-transit+at-rest with KMS. Can Redwood support customer-managed KMS in Dedicated or Private?
[01:26] Jordan: Yes - Dedicated supports customer KMS integrations and we can do Private with VPC + customer-managed KMS. Hosted can support strict retention and SSO but not customer KMS in the short-term.
[01:39] Ben (Data Eng): On workload sizing: our token mix is skewed - average prompt 120 tokens, response ~350 tokens, but some sessions blow out to 2k tokens. Burst arrivals at 30 requests/sec for 10 minutes during peak.
[01:53] Priya: That's helpful. For benchmarking we'll need a representative trace, latency percentiles, and top-k prompt set for quality checks. We'll run shot bursts to reproduce tail behavior; continuous batching helps average cost but hurts tail if queueing isn't tuned.
[02:08] Carlos: For success criteria: p50 < 120ms, p95 < 400ms, error rate <0.5%, and cost per 1k tokens under $X (we'll define). If we can't hit p95 on Hosted, we may prefer Dedicated or Private.
[02:23] Priya: Exactly. Our recommended pilot: 1) Week 0 - share test harness & trace; 2) Week 1 - hosted quick benchmark to get baseline; 3) Week 2 - Dedicated spinup with same workload for cost/latency comparison; 4) Week 3-4 - Private (if needed) or deeper tuning; decision gate end of week 4. That's a 4 week decision path, longer if deeper security reviews required.
[02:45] Asha: Can you quantify the expected latency improvement moving from Hosted->Dedicated->Private? ballpark numbers are fine.
[02:52] Priya: Ballpark: Hosted median is often low because of fast path, but p95 depends on multitenant noisy neighbors; Dedicated typically reduces p95 by ~20-40% depending on batch sizes and KV cache locality; Private can be similar to Dedicated or slightly better if co-located with your frontends and network is optimized. But Dedicated gives the best cost predictability.
[03:12] Carlos: How about autoscaling on Dedicated? We don't want sudden throttles during bursts.
[03:18] Jordan: Dedicated has configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity. You can set reserved baseline GPUs and allow automatic short-term burst capacity. We'll work with you to tune SLOs and upsizing thresholds.
[03:28] Ben: Any quick wins on cost - like quantization or batching recommendations we can try during pilot?
[03:33] Priya: Yes - we can provide model quantization profiles, recommended batch windows, and prefix/KV caching settings. We'll run A/B benchmarks: FP16 vs int8 quantized model throughput and quality delta. Expect 2-3x lower inference cost with aggressive quantization for some models, but you'll need to validate quality on your prompt set.
[03:54] Mei: Security caveat - for Private on-prem we have to ensure HSM integration, offline key wraps. That adds 2-3 weeks. Is that in scope?
[04:02] Jordan: We can do HSM/KMS integrations but they'll add time. That's why our pilot path runs Hosted first to validate functionality and then moves to Dedicated or Private for compliance.
[04:14] Tom: From procurement view, what's minimum commitment for Dedicated?
[04:18] Jordan: Typical pilot is a 1-3 month reserved capacity at a small commit level. We can make a short-term pilot contract for proof-of-value. Full commit discounts apply for 6-12 month contracts.
[04:28] Carlos: For benchmarks, what metrics will Redwood provide back?
[04:31] Priya: We'll deliver token-level latency distribution, cost per token, trace-level logs (sanitized), model quality evals on the prompt set, and per-route dashboards. We'll also share an estimate of unit economics across deployment modes.
[04:45] Asha: Network - we need to understand egress pattern and potential charges if Hosted crosses regions.
[04:50] Jordan: We'll include region-aware routing in the cost template and show egress assumptions. For Dedicated and Private you can keep data in-region.
[04:58] Ben: Small technical nit - your earlier doc mentioned KV cache and continuous batching. How sensitive is the cache to sequence length variance?
[05:05] Priya: KV cache effectiveness drops when you have very high variance or short-lived sessions, but for chat-like flows with reuse the cache can drastically cut token compute. We'll instrument cache hit rates in the benchmark.
[05:18] Carlos: Let's talk decision heuristics. If Hosted meets p95 and cost targets, go Hosted for speed. If Hosted meets latency but cost too high at scale, evaluate Dedicated. If Hosted fails security/KMS requirements, choose Dedicated or Private depending on VPC/KMS needs and procurement time. Does that map?
[05:35] Jordan: Yes, that's a good framing. We'll codify that into a simple decision matrix and share.
[05:41] Priya: Also include a rollback/fallback plan: e.g., start in Hosted with traffic shaping and fallback to a smaller model variant or lower-cost region if capacity/latency issues arise.
[05:53] Carlos: Timeline - we want production by mid-Jan; is that realistic?
[05:58] Jordan: If pilot starts late Oct and there are no heavy security blockers, a mid-Jan production for a single feature is plausible: pilot Oct-Nov, integration/validation Dec, rollout Jan. If Private on-prem or deep HSM work is required, add 4-8 weeks.
[06:14] Asha: Let's ensure we have a clear success criteria doc so security can sign off faster.
[06:18] Jordan: We'll produce a concise success criteria template with SLOs, quality thresholds, and required audit artifacts.
[06:24] Tom: Procurement needs an early estimate of run rate. Can you provide a best/worst case for 6 months?
[06:29] Priya: We'll run the cost model based on your trace and provide three scenarios: conservative (no quantization), expected (some quantization+caching), and aggressive (quant+cache+dedicated commit).
[06:40] Jordan: Quick recap / next steps: Jordan share pricing/commit doc; Priya share bench harness + sample model; Emberline to send traces and prompts; schedule benchmark kickoff wk of Oct 26.
[06:51] Carlos: Sounds good. Any risks we missed?
[06:54] Priya: Main risks are insufficient representative traces, network egress surprises, and longer security approvals for Private. We'll flag those early.
[07:05] Mei: Also dependency on front-end CDN proximity - co-locating inference closer to users helps latency.
[07:12] Jordan: Noted. We'll include network diagram examples.
[07:18] Tom: Alright thanks everyone.
[07:20] Carlos: Thanks both.
[07:22] Jordan: We'll follow up with docs and invite for the kickoff.

Note: occasional transcription errors present - e.g., "KV cash" or "K V cache" appears in automated notes, and speaker timestamps approximate.
